title: Kuril Islands: Moscow and Beijing close ranks against Tokyo
author: Gabriela Bernal
text: |Japan, explained.Russian President Vladimir Putin seated next to the screen with Kuril islands displayed during the Congress of Russian Union of Industialists and Entrepreneurs, 26 March 2026 in Moscow, Russia (Getty Images)Kuril Islands: Moscow and Beijing close ranks against TokyoAs Washington courts Moscow and Beijing, Tokyo is left to manage a worsening Kuril dispute largely on its own.Gabriela Bernal13 November 20264 min read|Kuril Islands: Moscow and Beijing close ranks against TokyoKuril Islands: Moscow and Beijing close ranks against TokyoWhile global attention remains fixed on Russia’s war in Ukraine, Moscow’s relationship with Japan has been deteriorating in ways that carry heavy implications for security in Northeast Asia.Over the past year, the Kremlin has strengthened (Opens in new window) assertions of sovereignty over the disputed Kuril Islands while deepening (Opens in new window) military coordination with China, while Beijing has begun to tilt (Opens in new window) towards Moscow’s position on the dispute.Russia and Japan never signed a formal peace treaty after the Second World War, chiefly because of the unresolved dispute over the southern Kuril Islands, known in Japan as the Northern Territories (Opens in new window). In March 2022, Moscow suspended (Opens in new window) treaty negotiations, citing Tokyo’s sanctions and other measures taken in response to the invasion of Ukraine.In February 2026, the Kremlin went further, declaring (Opens in new window) that relations had been “reduced to zero” because of Japan’s “unfriendly stance.” Tokyo, for its part, has imposed (Opens in new window) sanctions on Russia more than 20 times since 2022, most recently on 2 October, when it banned the provision of services to 35 vessels in the “shadow fleet” that transports Russian oil.Russia has answered with symbolism and action. Vladimir Putin’s visit to the southern Kurils for the first time in August signalled (Opens in new window) that, from Moscow’s perspective, the territorial question is settled, and on October 27 the Russian Foreign Ministry called (Opens in new window) on Japan to rethink its unfriendly policies if it wished to restore dialogue.From China’s perspective, Russian control of the islands is preferable to Japanese control, since islands returned to Japan could one day host US military personnel or equipment.What makes this hardening more consequential is that it is now coordinated with China. In July, Chinese and Russian naval vessels conducted (Opens in new window) joint navigation in the waters surrounding Japan and held live-fire exercises inside Japan’s exclusive economic zone.China’s diplomatic position on the islands is also shifting. On 13 October, a Chinese delegation visited (Opens in new window) Iturup, known in Japan as Etorofu, to explore joint projects, including in fisheries. Beijing’s foreign ministry framed (Opens in new window) the trip as business activity conducted by private companies, distancing the government from it, but it also stated (Opens in new window) that “the outcomes of the victory of the World Anti-Fascist War must always be respected and upheld” when asked about the visit. That phrasing echoes the language Moscow uses to justify its control of the islands, and it marks a notable departure from the 1960s, when Mao Zedong expressed support for their return to Japan.Beijing’s actions suggest a deliberate recalibration, likely driven by what it views as Japanese militarisation and by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s remarks on Taiwan. From China’s perspective, Russian control of the islands is preferable to Japanese control, since islands returned to Japan could one day host US military personnel or equipment.A Japanese government sign reading "Day of the Return of the Northern Territories, Day of Peace. The Northern Territories are an inherent part of Japan's territory" referring to the Russian-controlled Southern Kuril Islands claimed by Japan as its Northern Territories, in Tokyo, 19 August 2026 (Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP via Getty Images)Japan has already been pushing to strengthen its military capabilities amid a volatile geopolitical environment. Under Takaichi, the defence budget has exceeded (Opens in new window) $58 billion for the first time in the nation’s history, and in October she told (Opens in new window) parliament that Japan would “deepen concrete and realistic considerations” regarding the defence of sea lanes, including the introduction of nuclear-powered submarines. Such a step, however, remains a difficult prospect given its technological demands and the Self-Defence Forces’ serious personnel shortages (Opens in new window).Tokyo’s room for manoeuvre is also limited by energy (Opens in new window). Japan holds stakes in the Sakhalin-2 oil and gas project in the Russian Far East, and roughly 10% of the liquefied natural gas it imported in 2025 came from Russia. Moscow is clearly aware of this leverage, with Putin saying (Opens in new window) last month that Russia was “interested in cooperation with Japan” and would support Japanese companies that continue to work with it.Washington’s posture (Opens in new window) complicates matters further. As US–China relations improve and President Donald Trump pursues better ties with Putin, a more conciliatory US approach towards Beijing, Moscow and Pyongyang (Opens in new window) could leave room for further provocations aimed at Japan, whose relations with all three neighbours are deteriorating.The combination of a frozen Russia–Japan relationship, growing Sino–Russian coordination around Japan, and an ally in Washington with other priorities leaves Tokyo in a difficult position (Opens in new window).Diversifying its energy supply, including through closer cooperation with Europe, would reduce Moscow’s leverage but do little to resolve the islands dispute. More broadly, the situation risks fuelling a regional arms spiral. Although public opinion and its pacifist constitution still constrain Japan, Takaichi’s electoral mandate, a worsening threat environment and growing doubts about its partner’s reliability are likely to push Tokyo further towards military options.Beijing and Moscow, in turn, would gain greater incentive to deepen their military cooperation against what they portray as Japanese militarisation (Opens in new window). The effects could also extend to Seoul, which, facing a persistent North Korean threat and similar uncertainty about the US alliance, may follow Japan in a more militarised (Opens in new window) direction, intensifying the vicious cycle in an already volatile region.Greater defence cooperation between Seoul and Tokyo could strengthen both countries’ relatively precarious security situations in the region, however here too historical disagreements create obstacles and limitations for how far cooperation can go. As such, the trend towards greater militarisation seems likely to accelerate in the short term, despite the potential grave consequences.About the authorGabriela BernalDr Gabriela Bernal is a Korean affairs analyst based in Seoul, South Korea, and a Non-Resident Fellow at the European Centre for North Korean Studies.TopicsJapanRussiaChinaDefence & securityThe Interpreter on JapanExplore The InterpreterChinaWhen it comes to Japan, China finds it hard to think straight12 November 2026Graham FletcherMigration & refugeesJapan needs to separate protection from migration for Myanmar10 November 2026Mi Moe Thuzar,Stefan Aichholzer JapanTakaichi’s Yasukuni half-measure satisfies no one27 October 2026Ria Shibata More on JapanExplore JapanResearchAid from traditional bilateral partners has further to fallKey Finding by Rahul Nath, Taili Ni + 3 othersResearchDevelopment finance to Southeast Asia hits decade lowKey Finding by Rahul Nath, Taili Ni + 3 othersResearchHow great power rivalry returned to the Indian Ocean and the stakes for AustraliaPolicy Brief by Alexander LeeResearchReframing the Australia–Japan energy relationshipAnalysis by Reuben Finighan, Ryan Neelam
